blocks.content: 1. What Is a Single Point of Failure?
blocks.text: 1. What Is a Single Point of Failure?

blocks.content: A Single Point of Failure, SPOF, is any component in a system that, if it stops working, brings the entire system down with it. Finding and eliminating SPOFs is one of the most important, and most frequently overlooked, jobs in system design.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025893-873763550.png
blocks.alt: A SPOF has no backup and no alternative path, so its failure takes down whatever depends on it regardless of how well-built everything else is

blocks.content: A SPOF is a component with no backup, no redundancy, no alternative path. If it goes down, the whole system, or a critical part of it, becomes unavailable, regardless of how robust every other component happens to be.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271642129-758995953.png
blocks.alt: Ten redundant application servers are worthless the moment they all depend on one un-backed-up database

blocks.content: This is the trap that catches even careful designs: a team runs two application servers for redundancy, feels good about it, and never notices that both of those servers depend on a single database with no replica. The moment that database goes down, all the app-tier redundancy counts for exactly nothing.
2. Why SPOFs Are Dangerous
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271643900-423572785.png
blocks.alt: Most components eventually fail, and a SPOF means that inevitable bad day takes the whole system with it

blocks.content: Most components fail eventually: hardware wears out, software crashes, networks drop, people make mistakes. A SPOF means that when one specific component has its inevitable bad day, the entire system goes with it.

["Sudden failure, no warning: a SPOF can work perfectly for a long time and then suddenly stop. When it fails, the entire system can go down immediately, with users seeing errors and no backup available to absorb the impact","No automatic recovery: without a standby or replica already in place, recovering a SPOF means someone has to notice, diagnose, and manually fix or replace it, extending the outage for exactly as long as that takes"]
items: Sudden failure, no warning: a SPOF can work perfectly for a long time and then suddenly stop. When it fails, the entire system can go down immediately, with users seeing errors and no backup available to absorb the impact

No automatic recovery: without a standby or replica already in place, recovering a SPOF means someone has to notice, diagnose, and manually fix or replace it, extending the outage for exactly as long as that takes

blocks.content: 3. Common SPOFs in Real Systems

SPOFs hide in plain sight. These are the most common places they appear in production architectures, and even when some components are redundant, one single overlooked component can still bring down the entire application.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025568-845757186.png
blocks.alt: Six of the most common single points of failure found in real production systems

blocks.content: 1. Single DNS Provider
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025567-449771013.png
blocks.alt: A healthy fleet of servers is useless if users can never resolve the domain name to reach them

blocks.content: Problem: all traffic depends on one DNS provider resolving your domain. Why it's a SPOF: even if every server behind it is perfectly healthy, users cannot resolve your domain name to an IP address if that provider is down. Example: a user types myapp.com, but the DNS service is unavailable, so the browser cannot even locate your system in the first place.
2. Single Load Balancer
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271649580-166193824.png
blocks.alt: Ten healthy servers behind a single failed load balancer receive exactly zero traffic

blocks.content: Problem: all traffic passes through one load balancer. Why it's a SPOF: if the load balancer fails, requests never reach any application server behind it. Example: you have 10 healthy app servers, but a failed load balancer blocks all incoming traffic from ever reaching a single one of them.
3. Single Database (the Most Common SPOF)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025894-6307682.png
blocks.alt: Users can reach a perfectly healthy application, but nothing that touches data actually works

blocks.content: Problem: multiple application servers all depend on one database. Why it's a SPOF: if the database crashes, none of those app servers can read or write data. Example: users can reach the application, but login, payments, and data retrieval all stop working, because the single database behind them is unavailable. Why it's hard to eliminate: databases store critical state, so removing this SPOF requires real replication, failover, and consistency management, not just spinning up another instance.
4. Single Cache Node (Redis / Memcached)
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025895-421166558.png
blocks.alt: Losing a single cache node doesn't just remove the cache, it can overload the database sitting behind it

blocks.content: Problem: only one cache server is available. Why it's a SPOF: if the cache fails, every request that would have hit the cache goes directly to the database instead. Example: a website normally serves product data from Redis; Redis crashes, and millions of requests suddenly hit the database directly. Result: database overload and performance degradation, on top of losing the cache itself.
5. Single Message Queue / Broker

Problem: only one message broker handles asynchronous communication between services. Why it's a SPOF: if the broker fails, services cannot exchange messages at all. Example: an order service publishes events to a queue; if that queue is down, the payment, inventory, and notification services all stop receiving events, even though none of those services are themselves broken.
6. Single Availability Zone or Data Center
blocks.text: 6. Single Availability Zone or Data Center

blocks.content: Problem: everything runs in one physical location. Why it's a SPOF: a power outage, a network issue, or a natural disaster can take down the entire system at once. Example: all servers are hosted in one AWS Availability Zone; if that zone becomes unavailable, the entire application goes offline, regardless of how many redundant servers exist within that single zone.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
blocks.content: A system is only as reliable as its weakest, least-redundant component. Even with redundant application servers, a single DNS provider, load balancer, database, cache, message queue, or data center can still bring the entire system down on its own.

{"headers":["SPOF","Failure Trigger","What Breaks"],"rows":[["DNS Provider","Provider outage","Users cannot resolve the domain at all, no server is ever reached"],["Load Balancer","Hardware or process crash","Zero traffic reaches any backend server, however many exist"],["Database","Crash, disk failure, overload","Every read and write fails, the application appears broken end to end"],["Cache Node","Process crash, memory exhaustion","Traffic redirects to the database, which was never sized for full direct load"],["Message Broker","Crash, disk full","Asynchronous workflows silently stop, no new events are ever delivered"],["Availability Zone","Power, network, or disaster event","Every server in that zone becomes unreachable at once, together"]]}
4. Blast Radius: Not Every SPOF Is Equally Dangerous
blocks.text: 4. Blast Radius: Not Every SPOF Is Equally Dangerous

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271654535-656363836.png
blocks.alt: The same word, SPOF, describes both a catastrophic failure and a barely-noticed one, depending entirely on how much depends on it

blocks.content: A shared database backing the entire application and a dedicated backend behind one optional, rarely-used widget are both technically SPOFs, but they carry wildly different blast radii, how much of the system actually goes down when each one fails.

Blast radius is what should actually drive prioritization: a SPOF whose failure takes down checkout, login, and every core feature at once deserves fixing far sooner than a SPOF whose failure only disables one non-critical widget in a corner of the page. Section 3's six common SPOFs are not equally urgent for this exact reason, a single database's blast radius is almost always the entire application, while a single message broker's blast radius is scoped specifically to whatever asynchronous workflows depend on it.
5. Redundancy Isn't Free: The N+1 Pattern
blocks.text: 5. Redundancy Isn't Free: The N+1 Pattern

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025568-980426530.png
blocks.alt: Running exactly the capacity you need means losing even one instance already puts you over the edge

blocks.content: Adding a second instance of something is not automatically enough. If a system genuinely needs N servers to handle its normal load and only N are running, losing even one already puts the remaining servers over capacity, technically redundant, but still degraded or failing under the load spike a single loss creates.

The N+1 pattern, and its more conservative sibling N+2 for components that fail more often or take longer to replace, means intentionally running one more instance than the bare minimum normal load requires, so that losing one instance still leaves full capacity intact rather than merely avoiding total unavailability. This is exactly why a genuinely redundant load balancer pair, or a database cluster sized for N+1, costs more than the raw minimum two instances might suggest at first glance.

blocks.title: N+1 Is a Capacity Question, Not Just a Redundancy Question
blocks.content: Having two of something answers 'is there a backup'. Running N+1 answers a different, equally important question: 'when the backup is actually being used, is there still enough capacity left to serve normal load without degrading'.
6. How to Identify a SPOF
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025567-411024188.png
blocks.alt: Walking the request path and asking one question at every hop is the fastest way to find every SPOF in an architecture

blocks.content: The fastest way: draw the architecture and ask one question about every single component on it: is there only one of this? A more structured version of the same idea is to walk the request path from the user all the way to the data and back, asking that same question at every hop along the way.

In a typical diagram of this exercise, application servers that exist in pairs are marked safe, because if one dies, traffic simply moves to the other, while every component that exists as a single instance, the DNS provider, the load balancer, the database, gets marked as a SPOF. The same question, asked consistently at every hop, is what actually finds them.
7. How to Eliminate SPOFs
The answer is almost always the same at a high level, add redundancy, but exactly how that redundancy gets added differs meaningfully by component type.
Eliminating a Single Load Balancer
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025567-361649427.png
blocks.alt: An active-standby pair with a floating virtual IP removes the load balancer as a SPOF automatically

blocks.content: Run two load balancers, one active and one standby. A floating virtual IP switches to the standby automatically if the active one fails. Cloud providers, AWS ALB and GCP's load balancer among them, handle this failover automatically without any manual intervention.
Eliminating a Single Database
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025568-812030426.png
blocks.alt: A synced replica, ready to be promoted, is what actually removes a database as a SPOF

blocks.content: This is the hardest one to fix. Databases hold state, you cannot simply spin up another instance instantly and have it already contain the right data. The solution is replication: a primary handles writes while one or more replicas stay continuously in sync, and if the primary dies, a replica is promoted to take over as the new primary.
Eliminating a Single Cache Node

Use a Redis cluster, or a consistent-hashing pool of cache nodes covered in this module's dedicated Consistent Hashing topic. If one node fails, only the keys assigned specifically to it are lost, other nodes continue serving normally, and the system falls back to the database only for those specific missing keys rather than for every request.
Eliminating a Single Data Center
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025893-460159752.png
blocks.alt: Spreading across multiple zones means one zone's outage no longer means the whole system's outage

blocks.content: Deploy across multiple Availability Zones or regions, with traffic routed to whichever zones are currently healthy via DNS or a global load balancer, exactly the multi-region pattern also covered from the consistency angle in the CAP Theorem topic.
8. SPOFs Exist at Every Layer
The tricky thing about SPOFs: eliminate one, and there is often another one hiding right behind it. Removing SPOFs is not a single fix, it requires walking the entire stack, layer by layer.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025569-982448807.png
blocks.alt: Genuine high availability means every layer, not just the obvious ones, has its own backup

blocks.content: {"headers":["Layer","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["DNS","Two DNS providers serve the domain","If one DNS provider goes down, the other still resolves the domain, so users can still find the system"],["Load Balancer","One load balancer active, another on standby","If the active one fails, the standby automatically takes over routing traffic"],["Application Servers","Traffic spread across App 1, App 2, App 3","If one crashes, the load balancer simply stops sending it traffic and routes to the remaining healthy servers"],["Database","Primary handles reads and writes, replica stays synced","If the primary fails, the replica is promoted, and database failure no longer brings down the whole application"]]}

High availability is achieved exactly this way, by removing SPOFs at every layer rather than just the most obvious one. DNS, load balancers, application servers, and databases all need their own backup or replica, so that if any single component fails, another automatically takes over.
9. When Is a SPOF Acceptable?
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785271665171-319624831.png
blocks.alt: Eliminating every SPOF costs real money and real complexity, so the redundancy budget should go where failure actually costs the most

blocks.content: Eliminating every SPOF costs money and adds complexity. Not every system genuinely needs zero SPOFs, the right question is not "could this fail", every component could eventually fail, it is what the actual business cost of that specific component failing would be.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396025566-675092275.png
blocks.alt: One simple question separates an acceptable SPOF from one that genuinely needs to be fixed

blocks.content: If this component goes down at 2 AM on a Friday, and nobody notices until Monday morning, is that okay? If yes, a SPOF here may be acceptable. If the answer makes you uncomfortable, it's not.

A batch reporting job that runs once a night on a single worker is a very different risk than a single database backing a live checkout flow, even though both are technically SPOFs. Redundancy budget should go where the business cost of failure is actually highest, not spread evenly across every component regardless of what it does.

The example below implements the request-path-walking identification method from section 4 directly, as a real graph reachability check: given a dependency graph from user to database, it removes each component one at a time and checks whether the database is still reachable, correctly flagging the DNS server, load balancer, and database itself as SPOFs while confirming that neither individual app server is, since each has a working alternate path through the other.
Worked Example 1: A Startup's First Architecture
blocks.text: Worked Example 1: A Startup's First Architecture

blocks.content: A startup's architecture has two application servers behind one load balancer, both talking to one PostgreSQL database, with one Redis instance for caching, all hosted in a single AWS Availability Zone. Walking the request path: the DNS provider is a SPOF, the load balancer is a SPOF, the database is a SPOF, the Redis instance is a SPOF, and the entire Availability Zone is a SPOF, only the two application servers are actually redundant.

Given a limited budget, the team applies the 2 AM Friday test from section 9 to each one, weighted by blast radius from section 4. The database failing means checkout stops working entirely, unacceptable, so it gets a synced replica first. The load balancer failing means total downtime with no workaround, also unacceptable, so an active-standby pair with a floating IP comes next. The single Availability Zone is deliberately accepted as a SPOF for now, the team judges that risk acceptable until the business is large enough to justify the added cost and operational complexity of a full multi-region deployment.
Worked Example 2: Capacity Planning With N+1
blocks.text: Worked Example 2: Capacity Planning With N+1

blocks.content: A video streaming service measures that its transcoding pipeline needs exactly 8 worker instances to keep up with normal upload volume during peak hours. Running exactly 8 technically has redundancy in the sense that no single worker is a SPOF for the whole pipeline, one worker crashing does not stop transcoding entirely, but it does mean the remaining 7 workers are now running above their sustainable capacity, and the upload backlog starts growing.

Applying the N+1 pattern from section 5, the team runs 9 workers instead of 8. Losing any single worker now leaves exactly 8 running, still fully sufficient for normal peak load, and the backlog never grows in the first place. This is the concrete difference between a component merely having a backup and a system that has actually planned its capacity around losing one.
Common Mistakes

["Adding redundant application servers and assuming the system is now highly available, without checking whether they all still depend on one un-backed-up database","Treating SPOF elimination as a one-time exercise instead of walking the entire stack, since removing one SPOF frequently reveals another hiding directly behind it","Eliminating every possible SPOF regardless of actual business cost, spending redundancy budget evenly instead of where a failure would actually hurt the most, ignoring blast radius entirely","Forgetting that the cache layer itself can become a SPOF, and that losing it can silently overload the database sitting behind it","Calling a system redundant at N instances when it actually needs N to handle normal load, instead of running N+1 so that losing one instance does not immediately cause degradation"]
items: Adding redundant application servers and assuming the system is now highly available, without checking whether they all still depend on one un-backed-up database
Treating SPOF elimination as a one-time exercise instead of walking the entire stack, since removing one SPOF frequently reveals another hiding directly behind it
Eliminating every possible SPOF regardless of actual business cost, spending redundancy budget evenly instead of where a failure would actually hurt the most, ignoring blast radius entirely
Forgetting that the cache layer itself can become a SPOF, and that losing it can silently overload the database sitting behind it
Calling a system redundant at N instances when it actually needs N to handle normal load, instead of running N+1 so that losing one instance does not immediately cause degradation

blocks.content: Practice

Draw the architecture of a food delivery app: a mobile client, one DNS provider, one load balancer, three application servers, one PostgreSQL database, and one Redis cache, all in a single region. Walk the request path and list every SPOF you find.

For each SPOF identified, apply the 2 AM Friday test from section 9 and decide whether it is acceptable or must be fixed, and if it must be fixed, name the specific redundancy technique from section 7 that would fix it.

If that same app's three application servers are sized to exactly handle its measured peak load with all three running, explain, using the N+1 pattern from section 5, why that is a weaker setup than it first appears, even though no single server is technically a SPOF.
Key Takeaways

A single point of failure is any component with no backup or alternative path, whose failure takes down the whole system, or a critical part of it, regardless of how well-built everything else is. Redundancy elsewhere does not help if a SPOF exists anywhere along the request path, ten redundant application servers are worthless if they all depend on one un-backed-up database.

SPOFs commonly hide behind a single DNS provider, a single load balancer, a single database, a single cache node, a single message broker, and a single availability zone, each with a different blast radius and a different specific technique for eliminating it.

SPOFs are found by walking the request path end to end and asking, at every hop, whether there is only one of this component, and eliminated using a technique specific to that component type, active-standby pairs for load balancers, replication and promotion for databases, clustering for caches, multi-zone deployment for data centers. Not every SPOF needs fixing, the real question is always what a specific component's failure would actually cost the business, weighted by its blast radius, and redundancy itself is only complete once it is sized as N+1, not just N, so that using the backup does not itself become a new source of degradation.
The next topic, Latency vs Throughput vs Bandwidth, moves from availability concerns to the performance metrics that shape how a system is measured once it is actually reliable.
